# Attention, Worked Out

Source: https://pasekpasek.github.io/attention-worked-out/
Author: Paweł Pasek
Explains: Attention Is All You Need — Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit,
Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin, arXiv:1706.03762 [cs.CL], 2017

Attention is a weighted average where the weights are computed from the data itself. Everything else
in the paper — the scaling, the heads, the mask, the sinusoids — is a consequence of that one
sentence.

## 0. Where all this sits

Attention is one sub-layer inside a larger model, and reading about it without that frame is most of
what makes it hard.

Both stacks are six identical layers deep. An encoder layer has two sub-layers: multi-head
self-attention, then a position-wise fully connected feed-forward network. A decoder layer has three:
masked multi-head self-attention, then multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack —
queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder — then feed-forward. Every sub-layer is
wrapped as LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)), a residual connection followed by layer normalisation, which
is what makes a stack this deep trainable at all.

Below the stacks sit the embeddings, summed with the positional encoding; the decoder's output
embeddings are shifted right by one position. Above the decoder sit a learned linear transformation
and a softmax producing next-token probabilities.

Of that machine, this page opens the attention sub-layers and the positional encoding. The residual
connections, layer normalisation, feed-forward networks, embeddings and output head are real and
load-bearing, and out of scope here.

## 1. One head

In a self-attention layer — the case this page works through — every token produces three vectors,
all three from the same input through three learned projections:
a query (what am I looking for), a key (what do I offer) and a value (what do I pass on if chosen).
Token i scores every token j by q_i · k_j, softmaxes those scores into weights that sum to one, and
takes that weighted average of the values.

    Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q Kᵀ / √d_k ) V

Because the score is q_i · k_j with q = xW^Q and k = xW^K, it is a bilinear form:
x_i (W^Q W^Kᵀ) x_jᵀ. A head is therefore characterised by one matrix saying which kinds of token
attend to which. Different heads are different such matrices.

Each row of the attention matrix sums to exactly one. That is what makes the operation an average
rather than a sum, and it is guaranteed by the softmax rather than enforced afterwards.

## 2. Why divide by √d_k

The paper keeps two claims apart. Observed: additive attention beats unscaled dot-product attention
at larger d_k. Suspected, in the paper's own hedge: "we suspect that for large values of d_k, the dot
products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely
small gradients."

The arithmetic underneath is neither observed nor suspected but simply true, and the paper puts it in
a footnote: if the components of q and k are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1,
then their dot product q · k = Σ q_i k_i has mean 0 and variance d_k. Scores spread out as the head
gets wider, and the softmax of a wide spread is a spike. Dividing by √d_k returns the variance to 1 at
any width. At the paper's actual head width of 64, the unscaled softmax already puts
essentially all of its mass on a single key.

## 3. Multi-head

A single head averages everything into one distribution, and an average is where distinct relations
get blurred together. The fix is h attentions in parallel over narrower projections:

    MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head_1, …, head_h) W^O
           where head_i = Attention(Q W_i^Q, K W_i^K, V W_i^V)

The budget is the point. The paper uses h = 8 and d_k = d_v = d_model/h = 64, so eight heads of width
64 cost about what one head of width 512 would. You are not buying more computation; you are spending
the same computation on more than one question at a time.

## 4. The mask

Attention as defined lets every token see every other token, which is right when encoding a sentence
you already have. Generating one is different: while predicting position i the model must not have
seen i+1.

The fix is arithmetic, not architecture. Before the softmax, set every illegal score to −∞. Softmax
sends those to exactly zero, so the row renormalises over the positions that remain. Masking after
the softmax instead would leave rows summing to less than one, which is a quietly different model.

## 5. Attention cannot see order

Attention takes a set of vectors and returns a set: permute the inputs and every output permutes with
them, unchanged. There is no recurrence walking left to right and no convolution with a window, so
nothing in the mechanism knows which token came first. Shuffle the tokens with positional encoding
off and the output computed for a given token is bit-for-bit what it was, because its neighbours are
the same set.

The paper adds a fixed pattern to the embeddings rather than learning one:

    PE(pos, 2i)   = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d_model))
    PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d_model))

Wavelengths run from 2π up to 10000·2π, so low dimensions flip quickly and high ones barely move
across a whole sentence — a positional signal at every scale at once. The stated reason for choosing
sinusoids is relative position: for any fixed offset k, PE(pos+k) is a linear function of PE(pos),
which makes "three tokens back" something the model can learn to look for. The encoding attaches to
the slot, never to the word.

## 6. What this buys

    Layer type                  Complexity per layer   Sequential ops   Max path length
    Self-attention              O(n² · d)              O(1)             O(1)
    Recurrent                   O(n · d²)              O(n)             O(n)
    Convolutional               O(k · n · d²)          O(1)             O(log_k n)
    Self-attention (restricted) O(r · n · d)           O(1)             O(n/r)

The restricted row is a proposal, not a result: the paper offers it for very long sequences, notes it
raises maximum path length to O(n/r), and says the authors planned to investigate it in future work.
The model they train attends over everything.

The argument for replacing recurrence is not that attention is cheaper. Self-attention is the cheaper
layer only while n < d, which the paper notes is the common case for sentence-length sequences in
translation. The argument is that attention is shallow: two tokens at opposite ends of a sequence are
one operation apart rather than n apart, and gradients that travel a short path survive better than
gradients that travel a long one.

## What is real on this page, and what is not

Every number is computed in the browser from the formulas above: real softmax, real dot products,
real Gaussian sampling, real sinusoids, real complexity arithmetic. The projection matrices are toy
values, because the page ships no trained weights; they are chosen so the arithmetic stays inspectable
at d_model = 4 rather than 512.

## Out of scope

The mechanism, not the model. A full encoder–decoder stacks N = 6 of these layers on each side, and
every layer wraps its attention and its position-wise feed-forward network in a residual connection
and layer normalisation — LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)) — which is what makes a stack that deep
trainable. The decoder adds a second attention per layer, over the encoder's output. The training
recipe — warmup schedule, label smoothing, beam search — and the BLEU results are in the paper.
